You are Marina's husband, is that right? I am Elena. I have been sitting here rehearsing something to say to you for two courses.
Then we are in the same situation. I am Braulio. What were you rehearsing?
Something about the weather, which is why I gave up. Where are you from originally?
Sao Paulo. Although half of me is in Bahia now — I built a house there and I go every month.
Every month. If I had known that was possible, I would have done it years ago. I am from Milan, and I have been here eleven years.
Eleven years. Do you keep up with what is happening in Italy?
Obsessively. My husband says I read more Italian news than Italians do.
Then we have found some common ground, because I do the same with three newspapers every morning. Ask me anything about Brazilian politics.

Braulio, hi, it is Renata, Marina gave me your number. Listen, we are having a few people over on Saturday, about eight o'clock, and Marina said you might both come. It is nothing formal. There will be nine of us, and three of them are visiting from Lisbon, so most of the evening will be in English. I know Marina said you have been studying, so I thought I would tell you in advance instead of surprising you at the door. Bring nothing. Just come. Call me back when you can and let me know.

People complain that small talk is empty, and in one sense they are right. Nobody at a dinner table genuinely needs to know whether it rained this afternoon. But that is not what the question is for. The weather is a test signal. It says: I am open, I am friendly, and I am willing to spend thirty seconds on nothing in order to find out whether we have anything else. Researchers who study first conversations found that the topic almost never matters. What matters is the second question. Anybody can answer once. The person who asks you something back is the person who wants the conversation. So if you take one thing from this programme, take that. Do not worry about your opening line. Worry about your second question.

Elena introduces herself and admits she has been rehearsing something to say for two courses. Braulio tells her his name and asks what she was rehearsing. She says it was about the weather, and asks where he is from. He answers Sao Paulo, and mentions the house in Bahia and the ten days a month. Elena says she is from Milan and has been in Sao Paulo for eleven years, and the two of them find common ground in the news.
